To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the optimal solution for replication and routing is a function of the file popularity and that it scales in a way that depends on the file popularity distribution.

1) the optimal number of files to be stored in the network scales linearly with the number of nodes, 2) the optimal replication strategy is the same as in a conventional wireless network with random pairs, and 3) the required link capacity scales as O(√N).

(i) the number of files in the system scales with the square root of the number of nodes, (ii) the number of content replicas scales with the square of the number of files, (iii) the number of hops in a delivery path scales with the square-root of the number of content items, and (iv) the number of links that need to be used for content delivery scales with the number of files.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental limits of content delivery over multihop wireless ad hoc networks.
the fundamental question of how to efficiently replicate content over a multihop wireless network.
the design of efficient content distribution systems for wireless networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in a wireless network with M content items and N nodes, if the number of nodes N is larger than a critical value M^α, then the system can be operated at a constant capacity.
, in the regime of interest, the required link capacity scales as the square root of the number of nodes, i.e., the link capacity grows slower than √N.
the multihop paradigm can be used to scale the network to a large number of nodes, provided the file popularity is low enough, and the network is not too large.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
multihop communication can be sustainable for a large number of files, but only when the number of nodes is sufficiently large.
the network is sustainable as long as the number of files is not too large compared to the number of nodes.
the network is scalable if the number of nodes N and the number of files in the system M scale in a certain way.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for certain values of the file popularity parameter, content replication and multihop communication can be sustained with O(1) capacity.

multihop communication can be a sustainable paradigm for wireless networks, provided that the network is sufficiently large, that the content is popular enough and that the nodes have enough storage space.
, for certain file popularity regimes, the required link capacity can scale as O(1).
